generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, honest and balanced reflection matters because so much of the work can invite self-doubt: a practical that felt awkward, a placement interaction that did not go smoothly, a result that did not come out as predicted. A reflection that is all self-criticism, or all excuses, teaches you little. Looking at what went well as well as what did not, and owning your own part fairly, is what makes a psychologist's reflection genuinely useful.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students reflect on the same seminar in which their presentation of a research paper fell flat.

Tom writes only the negatives: 'I was terrible. I froze, I rushed, the whole thing was a disaster and everyone could tell. I am just not good at this.' This is honest about the difficulty, but it is one-sided and harsh. It names no positives, turns a single seminar into a verdict on him as a person, and offers nothing to build on.

Amara reflects on the same seminar in balance: 'The start was shaky and I rushed when I lost my place. But I had understood the paper's method well, and the point I made about the sample's lack of diversity landed, because two people picked it up. I froze mainly because I was reading from dense notes. Next time I will use short prompts instead.' This looks at the positives first, is honest about the difficulty without being cruel, and finds something to change.

Both found the seminar hard. Only Amara reflected in a way that was honest, balanced, and actually useful.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, a reflection is only useful when it is honest and balanced: looking at the positives first, never landing all on one side, and being truthful about your own part without being harsh. You can now explain why balance matters, tell a balanced reflection from a one-sided one, and recognise what makes a reflection honest rather than defensive or self-critical. With what reflection is, a simple model, and the honesty to use it well, you are ready to reflect on purpose.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reflection more balanced than Tom's?

items.text: It named what went well and what went badly, honestly and without being harsh.
It was more negative about her own ability.
It avoided mentioning anything that went wrong.
It was shorter and stuck to the facts.

feedback.correct: That's right. Naming both what went well and what went badly, fairly, makes it balanced.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. A balanced reflection includes both sides; which option does that?
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's reflection was balanced because it named the good and the bad honestly and fairly. Being more negative, or ignoring the negatives, is one-sided.
